source.title: Asymptotic Behavior of Adversarial Training in Binary Linear Classification
source.authors: Hossein Taheri; Ramtin Pedarsani; Christos Thrampoulidis

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; there are minor PDF/OCR artifacts, but no apparent truncation that prevents reading the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies the sampling ratio in binary classification and explicitly reports that the tested errors decrease rather than show double descent; it says the double-descent behavior is absent in its binary robust-classification setting.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own results for error versus sampling ratio δ=m/n, including behavior around an interpolation threshold. Results cited from other studies are not recorded. Sweeps over the adversarial-training parameter εtr are not rows because that parameter is not a claim axis. Figure values are not tabulated; the text describes their trends.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps the sampling ratio δ=m/n through the (robust) separability threshold for linear classifiers under adversarial training. It reports theory and simulation curves and explicitly states that double descent does not appear for any εtr, εts. That bears on the sample-wise version (V3) in a new setting, and the authors argue it as a contrast to double descent.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. More precisely: for convex decreasing losses such as hinge loss in binary robust classification, standard and adversarial errors fall steadily as δ grows. A sharp drop comes right after the robust-separability (interpolation) threshold, and no double descent appears for any εtr, εts. The authors contrast this with the double descent seen in adversarial linear regression with squared loss (JSH20).
record.recipe_differences: The study derives asymptotic predictions for regularized adversarial empirical risk minimization and illustrates error versus sampling ratio; it does not reproduce the original double-descent experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported trend is examined across Gaussian-mixture and signed-GLM data models and ℓ2/ℓ∞ attacks in the appendix; the main numerical illustration uses a hinge loss and isotropic Gaussian-mixture data.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
record.problems: The empirical numerical illustrations use n=200 and average over 20 experiments; the plotted error values are not tabulated in the text. The authors also present theoretical asymptotic results, but the numerical examples cover stylized binary models rather than deep networks or broad model classes.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant sampling-ratio rows identified. Results varying εtr and cited double-descent findings were excluded because they do not report a result on the claim's size, epoch, or sample-size axes.

untested.parts: No deep networks and no model-size sweep.
Capacity is not varied with the data distribution held fixed. Only the sample ratio at fixed n=200 is swept, so whether risk improves again past interpolation as capacity grows is not tested.
No effective-complexity measure is proposed or tested.
No label-noise manipulation, no multiple-peak analysis, and no comparison of tuned versus untuned ridge regularization. The GMM curves use a single small ridge, r=1e-4.

missing.what: GMM with ℓ2 attacks: errors decrease as δ increases, with adversarial error approaching the Bayes error; curves are shown for several δ values
Universality check (Rademacher vs Gaussian mixture, q=∞, εtr=εts=1). The x-axis may be δ, but this is not stated in the text; worth checking for a sample-axis curve

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Reader states r1–r6 as reversed; changed to absent or cannot_determine, since decreasing error with more data is not the opposite of 'more data can hurt' at a peak. The r=0 GLM curves exist only above the separability threshold, so they cannot speak to a peak. V4 dropped as untested because δ is varied by sample count at fixed n. The GMM analysis uses ridge r=1e-4; any regularization can damp a peak, so the absence may partly reflect regularization (relevant to V6, but not tested). Figure values are not tabulated.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over training epochs or training time.
Tested through sampling-ratio sweeps in the paper's stylized binary classification settings, not across general datasets or model families.
Tested only in the studied binary linear-classification/robust-training settings, not across model classes generally.
No single effective-complexity measure is proposed or tested as predicting peak locations across axes.
No study of label-noise-driven peaks, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
No comparison of the curve under an alternative effective parameter count.
